title: From court innovation to public memory
paragraphs: The later history of Hangul was neither immediate universal acceptance nor a single uninterrupted triumph. Classical Chinese retained great prestige in many elite contexts, while vernacular writing expanded across different genres and audiences over time. The changing balance between scripts was linked to education, gender, literature, administration, and the wider social world.

Under modern colonial rule, language and script became bound to questions of cultural survival and identity. In contemporary Korea, Hangul carries immense public symbolic significance, though modern everyday use is shaped by national division, regional variation, technological change, and standardization. These later developments belong to their own historical units rather than being collapsed into the invention story.

The invention of a writing system is an ideal example of the larger KOREA reading experience. A reader can begin with a single question—why did Sejong commission a script?—and follow paths into phonetics, royal government, print culture, women’s letters, colonial language politics, and digital Korean today.
